extracted_claims.text: AI systems used for recruitment and selection of candidates (e.g., resume screening, ranking, targeted job ads) and for other employment/worker-management decisions are classified as 'high-risk' under Annex III of the EU AI Act.

Providers of high-risk AI systems must implement a risk-management system, data governance measures, technical documentation, automatic logging, transparency/instructions for use, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity measures (Articles 9-15).
Providers of high-risk AI systems must maintain a quality management system covering regulatory-compliance strategy, testing, and change-management procedures (Article 17).

Providers must undergo a conformity assessment, issue an EU declaration of conformity, affix CE marking, register the system in the EU database, and take corrective action/report serious incidents (Articles 16, 43, 25, 26, 20).
Deployers of high-risk AI systems used in employment must conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) under Article 27.
High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow effective human oversight, and deployers must ensure such oversight is exercised in practice (Article 14).

Deployers must use the system per the provider's instructions, monitor its operation, keep logs, and in employment contexts inform workers/representatives before use; some sources also describe complementary GDPR obligations (e.g., DPIAs, Article 22 right to human review) though these are separate from the AI Act itself.
Prohibited AI practices (Article 5) — 8 of the 9 listed practices — became effective on 2 February 2025; a ninth prohibition (introduced via the AI Omnibus) takes effect in December 2026.
Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models entered into application on 2 August 2025, with Commission enforcement powers over GPAI providers activating 2 August 2026.
Under the AI Act as originally adopted, high-risk AI system obligations (Annex III, including employment/recruitment systems) were scheduled to become fully applicable on 2 August 2026.

In November 2025 the European Commission proposed a 'Digital Omnibus' to delay application of high-risk (Annex III) rules by up to 16 months, tying the start date to confirmation that needed standards and tools are available.
On 7 May 2026 the Council and Parliament reached political agreement to simplify and streamline AI Act rules, including adjusting the high-risk implementation timeline.

The Digital Omnibus on AI entered into force on 27 July 2026, revising the application date for Annex III high-risk systems (including employment/recruitment tools) to 2 December 2027, and for Annex I high-risk systems embedded in regulated products to 2 August 2028.

On 2 August 2026 the Commission's AI Office and national market surveillance authorities began enforcing AI Act rules that did take effect on that date — chiefly Article 50 transparency obligations and GPAI provider obligations — not the Annex III high-risk employment obligations, which remain pending until 2 December 2027.

The AI Office (within the European Commission) and national market surveillance authorities share investigative and sanctioning powers for enforcing the AI Act, including high-risk AI rules once they apply; the AI Office has powers to send requests for information and impose fines for incorrect or misleading replies.

Penalty tiers under the AI Act scale with violation type: non-compliance with prohibited AI practices carries the highest fines; non-compliance with data-governance/transparency requirements for high-risk systems and other high-risk requirements carry lower, tiered fines.

On 19 May 2026 the European Commission published draft guidelines on classification of high-risk AI systems (including employment-related Annex III categories) to help providers, deployers, and market surveillance authorities determine high-risk status.

# EU AI Act Compliance for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools: Requirements and Enforcement Status

## Executive Summary
AI recruitment and worker-management tools are classified as "high-risk" under Annex III of the EU AI Act, triggering extensive provider and deployer obligations (high confidence) ([FRA](https://fra.europa.eu/en/project/2023/assessing-high-risk-artificial-intelligence), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3)). However, the applicable deadline for these obligations has shifted repeatedly: originally set for 2 August 2026, it was pushed to 2 December 2027 via the "Digital Omnibus" that entered into force 27 July 2026 (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy EC](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-high-risk-systems), [Gibson Dunn](https://www.gibsondunn.com/eu-ai-act-omnibus-agreement-postponed-high-risk-deadlines-and-other-key-changes)). As of the sources reviewed, no enforcement actions, fines, or investigations have been documented specifically against AI hiring/recruitment tool providers or deployers (high confidence) ([Commission](https://commission.europa.eu/news-and-media/news/safer-and-more-transparent-ai-2026-08-02_en)).

## Key Findings

### Classification
AI systems used for resume screening, candidate ranking, targeted job advertising, and other employment/worker-management decisions are classified as high-risk under Annex III (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3), [Warden AI](https://www.warden-ai.com/resources/eu-ai-act-hiring-recruitment)). Draft Commission guidelines on classifying high-risk systems in employment were published 19 May 2026 to help providers and deployers determine status (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy EC](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/draft-commission-guidelines-classification-high-risk-ai-systems), [Jones Day](https://www.jonesday.com/en/insights/2026/06/draft-eu-guidelines-clarify-when-ai-systems-are-highrisk-under-the-ai-act)).

### Provider Obligations
Providers must implement a risk-management system, data governance measures, technical documentation, automatic logging, transparency/instructions for use, human oversight design, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity measures under Articles 9–15 (high confidence) ([HeyMilo](https://www.heymilo.ai/blog/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know), [Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20)). They must also maintain a quality management system under Article 17 (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-17)), undergo conformity assessment, issue an EU declaration of conformity, affix CE marking, register in the EU database, and report serious incidents under Articles 16, 20, 25, 26, and 43 (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-16), [AO Shearman](https://www.aoshearman.com/en/insights/ao-shearman-on-tech/zooming-in-on-ai-10-eu-ai-act-what-are-the-obligations-for-high-risk-ai-systems)).

### Deployer Obligations
Deployers must conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) under Article 27, though this is only medium confidence given corroboration variance (medium confidence) ([Secure Privacy](https://secureprivacy.ai/blog/fria-fundamental-rights-impact-assessment-ai), [activeMind.legal](https://www.activemind.legal/guides/fundamental-rights-impact-assessment)). Systems must be designed for effective human oversight, and deployers must ensure that oversight is exercised in practice under Article 14 (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-14)). Some sources also note deployers should follow provider instructions, monitor operation, keep logs, and inform workers before use, alongside separate GDPR duties such as DPIAs and Article 22 rights — though these latter obligations are low confidence and distinct from the AI Act itself (low confidence) ([Iris Global](https://www.irisglobal.com/blog/payroll/eu-ai-act-hr-compliance-guide), [Crowell & Moring](https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/artificial-intelligence-and-human-resources-in-the-eu-a-2026-legal-overview)).

### Timeline
Prohibited AI practices (Article 5) took effect 2 February 2025, with a ninth prohibition arriving via Omnibus in December 2026 (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy EC](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai)). GPAI provider obligations applied from 2 August 2025, with Commission enforcement powers activating 2 August 2026 (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/faq)). Annex III high-risk obligations, originally due 2 August 2026, were postponed via the Digital Omnibus (proposed November 2025, agreed 7 May 2026, in force 27 July 2026) to 2 December 2027 (high confidence) ([Gibson Dunn](https://www.gibsondunn.com/eu-ai-act-omnibus-agreement-postponed-high-risk-deadlines-and-other-key-changes), [Consilium](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/05/07/artificial-intelligence-council-and-parliament-agree-to-simplify-and-streamline-rules)).

### Penalties
Penalty tiers scale by violation type, with prohibited-practice breaches carrying the highest fines and high-risk data-governance/transparency breaches carrying lower tiered fines (high confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/nl/european-ai-alliance/best-practices/eu-ai-act-10-things-high-risk-companies-need-do), [Holistic AI](https://www.holisticai.com/blog/penalties-of-the-eu-ai-act)).

### Enforcement
The AI Office and national market surveillance authorities began enforcing the provisions that took effect 2 August 2026 (transparency and GPAI rules), not the Annex III employment obligations, which remain pending (high confidence) ([Commission](https://commission.europa.eu/news-and-media/news/safer-and-more-transparent-ai-2026-08-02_en)). No documented enforcement actions have targeted AI hiring/recruitment tools specifically (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy EC](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/european-approach-artificial-intelligence)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on whether the August 2026 deadline still applies or was superseded by the Digital Omnibus (Cloud Security Alliance vs. Questa AI, Belgravewhitmore vs. Digital Strategy EC). The exact top penalty cap is inconsistently reported as €35 million or €40 million (Futurium vs. EU AI Act key issues page). The FRIA requirement (claim_005) carries only medium confidence, and claim_007 on deployer/GDPR overlap is low confidence and should be treated cautiously.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear how "significant modification" rules will apply to hiring tools placed on market before the new 2027 deadline. The interaction between AI Act deployer duties and GDPR obligations (DPIAs, Article 22) is not fully resolved. The final adoption status of the draft May 2026 classification guidelines is unknown. Given the current date precedes the 2 December 2027 application date, it is unresolved whether any enforcement or transitional compliance expectations will emerge before then.

report:
# EU AI Act vs. US Federal AI Policy: Foundation Model Governance Compared

## Executive Summary
The EU has established a binding, enforceable regulatory regime for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models under the AI Act, with dedicated enforcement infrastructure and significant penalties (high confidence). By contrast, US federal policy relies on executive orders, voluntary frameworks, and stalled legislation, with no comprehensive statute governing foundation model providers (high confidence). This creates a stark asymmetry: binding EU obligations already in force versus a patchwork of voluntary US mechanisms and pending bills.

## Key Findings

### EU: Binding Legal Obligations
The AI Act imposes legally enforceable duties on GPAI providers under Article 53, including technical documentation, information-sharing with downstream deployers, a copyright policy, and training-data summaries ([Article 53, AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)) (high confidence). Models classified as posing "systemic risk" (e.g., trained above 10^25 FLOPs) face additional Article 55 duties: adversarial testing, risk mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity measures ([Orrick AI Law Center](https://ai-law-center.orrick.com/eu-ai-act/general-purpose-ai)) (medium confidence). Open-source GPAI models receive partial exemptions from documentation rules unless deemed systemic-risk ([Article 53](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)) (high confidence). These obligations took effect 2 August 2025 ([European Commission](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/eu-rules-general-purpose-ai-models-start-apply-bringing-more-transparency-safety-and-accountability)) (high confidence), with high-risk system rules following 2 August 2026 ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/timeline/timeline-implementation-eu-ai-act)) (high confidence). A May 2026 "omnibus" agreement streamlined certain deadlines, including postponing sandbox requirements to 2027 ([Council of the EU](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/05/07/artificial-intelligence-council-and-parliament-agree-to-simplify-and-streamline-rules)) (high confidence).

A voluntary General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, developed via multi-stakeholder process, offers a presumption of conformity for signatories and lighter Commission scrutiny ([EC Code of Practice policy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents-code-gpai)) (high confidence), though it was published 10 July 2025—after the Act's own 2 May 2025 statutory deadline ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-Purpose_AI_Code_of_Practice)) (high confidence).

### EU: Enforcement and Penalties
The European AI Office holds exclusive competence over GPAI enforcement, separate from decentralized national authorities handling high-risk systems ([EC AI Office](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-office)) (high confidence). Non-compliance can trigger fines up to 3% of global turnover or €15 million ([Cyberhaven](https://www.cyberhaven.com/infosec-essentials/eu-ai-act)) (high confidence), with other tiers reaching €35 million/7% for prohibited practices (low confidence, per [Cyberhaven](https://www.cyberhaven.com/infosec-essentials/eu-ai-act)).

### US: Voluntary and Fragmented Approach
US federal AI governance rests on executive orders, agency guidance, and voluntary frameworks rather than a single statute ([European Parliament study](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/778575/ECTI_STU(2025)778575_EN.pdf)) (high confidence). A June 2, 2026 executive order ("Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security") directs agencies to strengthen cybersecurity and establishes a voluntary framework for "covered frontier models," including optional 30-day pre-release government access ([McDermott Will & Emery](https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/new-executive-order-shifts-us-ai-policy-toward-national-security)) (high confidence for the EO; medium confidence for voluntary-access details). The NIST AI Risk Management Framework remains voluntary, though it informs procurement and state affirmative-defense provisions like Colorado's AI Act ([NeuralTrust](https://neuraltrust.ai/blog/nist-ai-rmf-implementation-guide)) (high confidence). Bipartisan legislation—the AI Foundation Model Transparency Act of 2026 (H.R. 8094)—was introduced March 26, 2026, to direct FTC disclosure rules on training data ([Rep. Beyer's office](https://beyer.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=9013)) (high confidence), but remains pending in committee, unenacted ([Congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/8094/text)) (medium confidence). A prior 2023 version by Rep. Beyer similarly failed to pass (low confidence, [EP copyright study](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/meetdocs/2024_2029/plmrep/COMMITTEES/JURI/DV/2025/05-12/2025.05.12_item6_Study_GenAIfromacopyrightperspective_EN.pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the exact title of the June 2026 executive order ("Safety" vs. "Security") though the signing date is consistent. Terminology around AI Act "entry into force" versus "entry into application" is used inconsistently across EU sources, risking confusion about effective dates. Several low-confidence claims deserve caution: the characterization of US federal policy as entirely lacking binding requirements ([3CL analysis](https://www.3cl.org/the-eu-ai-act-and-usa-ai-gov-action-plan-a-legal-comparison), 0.17 confidence), the claim about "ideologically neutral" AI procurement orders (0.68 confidence but single-source), and the 2027 full-compliance deadline for pre-2025 GPAI models (0.12 confidence, single source).

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear how the May 2026 omnibus agreement formally amends Article 53/55 obligations already in force. The legislative trajectory of H.R. 8094 is unconfirmed beyond introduction. The technical threshold defining "covered frontier models" under the June 2026 EO is undisclosed, pending a classified benchmarking process. No source assesses actual enforcement outcomes (fines levied) under the EU regime versus comparable US mechanisms, nor how multinational firms would reconcile EU binding obligations with the voluntary US framework.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes a dual-track conformity assessment system for high-risk AI systems: sectoral-legislation-based assessment for Annex I products and largely internal control for Annex III systems, with third-party notified body review reserved mainly for biometric systems (high confidence). As of late 2026, however, the notified body ecosystem remains underdeveloped, with no source able to confirm a specific count of AI Act-designated bodies, and the compliance timeline itself has shifted following the June 2026 Digital Omnibus extension (high confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Under Article 43, high-risk AI systems already covered by EU harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally assessing AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). For Annex III high-risk systems (points 2–8), the general route is internal control by the provider under Annex VI, without notified body involvement, though this claim carries only low confidence due to weaker sourcing (low confidence) ([FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). By contrast, for Annex III point 1 (biometric) systems that apply harmonised standards, providers may choose between internal control (with conditions) or third-party assessment by a notified body reviewing the quality management system and technical documentation (medium confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Conformity assessment itself is defined in Article 3(20) as demonstrating fulfilment of Chapter III Section 2 requirements (medium confidence) ([Article 3](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-3)).

Certificates are valid up to five years (Annex I) or four years (Annex III), renewable, and can be suspended or withdrawn by notified bodies subject to appeal, though this rests on a single lower-authority source (low confidence) ([GovernanceDocs](https://governancedocs.com/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). Substantial system modifications trigger a new assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Notified bodies may, as a last resort under Annex VII, access training data and trained models to verify Chapter III Section 2 compliance, subject to IP/confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation
Notified bodies must be designated by a national notifying authority (Article 28) via a notification procedure (Article 30) verifying independence and competence requirements (Article 31), and are assigned identification numbers listed in the NANDO database (Article 35) (high confidence) ([Article 28](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-28), [Article 35](http://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-35)). Article 31 requires independence from providers, economic-interest operators, and competitors (medium confidence) ([Article 31](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-31)). Bodies already notified under sectoral legislation (Annex I, Section A) may assess AI Act requirements if their compliance with specific Article 31 sub-provisions is verified during notification (high confidence, per EUR-Lex) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng)). A Council document (ST-7322-2026) proposes an "AIP" coding system to scope designation of conformity assessment bodies by Annex I category (medium confidence) ([Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Standards, Documentation, and Deadlines
Compliance with harmonised CEN-CENELEC (JTC 21) standards creates a legal presumption of conformity (Article 40) (high confidence) ([Article 40](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-40)); the Commission mandated this standardisation work in May 2023 (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-act-standardisation)). Providers must retain technical documentation and conformity records for 10 years (high confidence) ([Article 11](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-11)), and issue an EU declaration of conformity per Article 47 (medium confidence) ([Article 47](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-47)). The June 2026 Digital Omnibus extended the Annex III compliance deadline from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and Annex I deadline from 2027 to 2028 (high confidence) ([CSA](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-omnibus-vii-deadline-delay-20260)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Older sources still cite 2 August 2026 as the binding deadline for Annex III obligations, while updated sources confirm this was pushed to December 2027 ([Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment-requirements-process-guide) vs. [CSA](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-omnibus-vii-deadline-delay-20260)). Sources also disagree on how advanced notified body designation is: one (low confidence, 0.12) says "very few" bodies are designated ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)), while another (low confidence, 0.12) describes the pool as merely "still forming" ([GovernanceDocs](https://governancedocs.com/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). Claims about Annex III internal-control defaults, certificate validity periods, and Ireland's national implementation model are all flagged low-to-medium confidence (0.12–0.42) due to thin sourcing.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source provides a current count or list of AI Act-specific designated notified bodies, nor clarity on which Member States have completed Article 30 notifications. The finalization status of CEN-CENELEC harmonised standards in the Official Journal is undocumented, as is the adoption status of the Council's AIP coding system. The interaction between GPAI models embedded in high-risk systems and conformity assessment procedures remains unaddressed.

extracted_claims.text: As originally adopted, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act) entered into force on 1 August 2024, and under Article 113 the general application date, including for high-risk AI obligations, was set at 2 August 2026 (36 months after entry into force).

The Digital Omnibus on AI, which reached trilogue agreement on 7 May 2026, was approved by the European Parliament on 11 June 2026, received final Council approval on 29 June 2026, and entered into force as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 on 27 July 2026, amending the AI Act's implementation timetable.

Under the amended AI Act (post Digital Omnibus), the obligations for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III (standalone high-risk systems under Article 6(2)) now apply from 2 December 2027, extended from the original 2 August 2026 date.

High-risk AI systems that are safety components of, or themselves constitute, products already regulated under EU harmonisation legislation (Annex I systems) will be subject to obligations from 2 August 2028, extended from the original 2 August 2027 date.

Prior to the Digital Omnibus being finalized, the delay to Annex III obligations was described by the Commission as a proposal, with possible timelines of 6–12 months after adoption of relevant technical standards, or a fixed date of 2 December 2027.
The Commission's November 2025 proposal (COM(2025)836) discussed grace-period provisions for high-risk AI systems already lawfully placed on the market before the relevant Article 111(2) date.

Operators of high-risk AI systems (other than those in large-scale IT systems under Annex X) that were placed on the market or put into service before the relevant date are subject to the Regulation only if the systems undergo significant design changes after that date; in any case providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for use by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030.

Some general regulatory timeline explanations state that most AI Act obligations, including high-risk rules for Annex III systems, were originally scheduled to apply from 2 August 2026, without reflecting the later Digital Omnibus extension.

Separately from Annex III, AI systems that are components of large-scale IT systems listed in Annex X and placed on the market before 2 August 2027 must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030.

Registration of high-risk AI systems and their providers/deployers in the EU database (Article 71) must occur before the system listed in Annex III is placed on the market or put into service, except for certain critical-infrastructure systems.

Providers of high-risk AI systems face fines of up to €15 million or 3% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher) under Article 99(4) for non-compliance, with a lower cap for SMEs under Article 99(6).

Annex III currently lists eight categories of standalone high-risk AI systems, including biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice, subject to amendment by the Commission.

# When Do Annex III High-Risk AI System Obligations Apply Under the EU AI Act?

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act's obligations for standalone high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III originally were set to apply from 2 August 2026, but this deadline has been extended to **2 December 2027** following adoption of the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), which entered into force 27 July 2026 (high confidence). Related deadlines have also shifted: Annex I product-safety-linked high-risk systems now face obligations from 2 August 2028, and public-authority deployers/providers must comply by 2 August 2030 (high confidence).

## Key Findings

### Original Timeline (Pre-Amendment)
As originally adopted, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 entered into force on 1 August 2024, with Article 113 setting general application—including Annex III high-risk obligations—at 2 August 2026, 36 months after entry into force (high confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/topics/en/article/20230601STO93804/eu-ai-act-first-regulation-on-artificial-intelligence), [Publications Office](http://publications.europa.eu/resource/cellar/dc8116a1-3fe6-11ef-865a-01aa75ed71a1.0006.03/DOC_1)).

### The Digital Omnibus Amendment
The Digital Omnibus on AI progressed through trilogue agreement (7 May 2026), European Parliament approval (11 June 2026), Council approval (29 June 2026), and entry into force as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 on 27 July 2026, amending the AI Act's implementation schedule (high confidence) ([European Parliament Legislative Train](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-internal-market-and-consumer-protection-imco/file-digital-omnibus-on-ai), [Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-omnibus-vii-deadline-delay-20260)).

### Current Applicable Dates
Under the amended Act, Annex III standalone high-risk system obligations now apply from **2 December 2027**, a roughly 16-month extension from the original date (high confidence) ([EC AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-ai-act-go-effect-what-its-timeline-implementation), [Digital Strategy EC](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ai-omnibus-enters-force)). Annex I high-risk systems (safety components of already-regulated products) now face obligations from **2 August 2028**, delayed from 2 August 2027 (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy EC](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ai-omnibus-enters-force), [Gibson Dunn](https://www.gibsondunn.com/eu-ai-act-omnibus-agreement-postponed-high-risk-deadlines-and-other-key-changes)).

### Additional Transitional and Deployer-Specific Provisions
Providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for use by public authorities must comply by **2 August 2030**, and operators of systems already on the market before the relevant date generally remain subject to obligations only if the system undergoes significant design changes afterward (high confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). AI systems that are components of large-scale IT systems listed in Annex X, if placed on the market before 2 August 2027, must achieve compliance by **31 December 2030** (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex consolidated text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727)). Registration in the EU database (Article 71) must occur before an Annex III system is placed on the market or put into service, with exceptions for certain critical-infrastructure systems (high confidence) ([EC AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-71)). Annex III currently enumerates eight categories of high-risk systems—biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice—subject to Commission amendment (high confidence) ([EC AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3)).

### Penalties
Non-compliant providers of high-risk systems reportedly face fines up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover under Article 99(4), with lower caps for SMEs (low confidence) ([Vigilia](https://aivigilia.com/blog/eu-ai-act-annex-iii-high-risk-ai-systems-list)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Some sources still cite the original 2 August 2026 date without reflecting the Digital Omnibus extension, creating apparent conflict with post-amendment sources citing 2 December 2027 (low confidence claim) ([Snowflake](https://www.snowflake.com/en/artificial-intelligence/ai-governance/eu-ai-act) vs. [Questa AI](https://www.questa-ai.com/privacy-cafe/eu-ai-act-countdown-is-your-annex-iii-system-ready-for-august-2)). One source frames the December 2027 date as merely one option under a pending Commission proposal rather than a confirmed date—reflecting differing legislative stages captured across sources (low confidence) ([LinkedIn/Oliver Patel](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/oliver-patel_when-will-eu-ai-act-high-risk-ai-compliance-activity-7401984085377830912-RglO)). Sources also diverge on exact grandfathering/transitional dates under Article 111, likely due to amendment timing inconsistencies between pre- and post-Omnibus texts.

## Knowledge Gaps
Unresolved questions include: whether technical standards and national competent authorities will be operational in time for the 2 December 2027 deadline; the precise definition of "significant design changes" triggering compliance for legacy systems; the final consolidated wording of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amending Articles 111 and 113; and whether further political or legal challenges could still alter the 2 December 2027 or 2 August 2028 dates. The interaction between the 2 August 2030 public-authority deadline and the general Annex III deadline also requires clarification.
